This reframing avoids malformed figures and makes the design claim broader than local habitability.

fields.before: Boteach’s willingness to be angry at God can become an argument from moral protest rather than a denial of suffering. Condemnation of apparently pointless suffering presupposes standards that outrun power, custom, and personal preference; the theist may interpret protest as engagement with a real moral source whose goodness makes lament intelligible. The difficulty is formidable: relationship does not excuse divine silence, and protest may fit secular moral realism equally well. Still, this approach takes hiddenness seriously while explaining why faith can include accusation instead of easy providential reassurance.
